opening: Before working out a strategy for a game, check whether there is anything to work out.

steps.prompt: A chocolate bar of 2 by 3 squares. A move breaks one piece into two along a line. How many breaks are made before it is all single squares, whatever order they are made in?
nudges: How many pieces are there at the start and at the end, and what does one break do to that number?
steps.showed: Each break adds one piece: from 1 piece to 6.

steps.prompt: Two players take turns breaking; whoever makes the last break wins. Who wins the 2 by 3 bar?
options: The first player, whatever either of them does
steps.showed: Five breaks, and the first player makes the odd-numbered ones.

steps.prompt: The numbers 1 to 10 are on a board. A move erases two of them and writes their sum. The game stops when one number is left. How many moves are made?
nudges: What does a move do to how many numbers are on the board?

steps.prompt: A heap of 15 stones. A move splits one heap into two non-empty heaps. The player who cannot move loses. Who wins?
nudges: How many heaps are there at the end, and how does a move change the number of heaps?
steps.showed: From 1 heap to 15 heaps takes exactly 14 moves, an even number, so the second player makes the last one.

steps.prompt: A tree has 8 vertices. A move removes a vertex that has exactly one neighbour (and its edge). The game ends when a single vertex is left. How many moves are made?
nudges: Is there always a vertex with exactly one neighbour while at least two vertices remain?
steps.showed: A tree with two or more vertices always has a leaf, so the game cannot stop early: 7 moves.

steps.prompt: A convex hexagon. A move draws a diagonal that does not cross any diagonal already drawn. The player who cannot move loses. How many diagonals are drawn in the whole game, however it is played?
steps.verify:
import itertools
diag = [(a, b) for a, b in itertools.combinations(range(6), 2) if (b - a) % 6 not in (1, 5)]
cross = lambda p, q: len({*p, *q}) == 4 and (p[0] < q[0] < p[1]) != (p[0] < q[1] < p[1])
sizes = set()
def go(chosen):
    free = [d for d in diag if d not in chosen and not any(cross(d, c) for c in chosen)]
    if not free: sizes.add(len(chosen)); return
    for d in free: go(chosen + [d])
go([])
result = sizes.pop() if len(sizes) == 1 else None
nudges: When no more diagonals fit, into what shapes is the hexagon cut, and how many of them are there?
steps.showed: The game ends with the hexagon cut into triangles: always 4 triangles and 3 diagonals. So the first player wins.

steps.prompt: A pile of 10 stones; a move removes 1 or 2; whoever takes the last stone wins. Does the same reasoning settle it?
options: No: the number of moves depends on the choices made, so parity alone decides nothing
Yes: the first player wins because 10 is even
nudges: Can this game last 5 moves? Can it last 10?
steps.showed: Between 5 and 10 moves are possible. When the length is not forced, you really do have to label positions.

steps.prompt: Faced with a new game in a contest, which check comes first?
options: Does some count change by exactly one with every move and decide when the game ends? If so, only its parity matters
Compute the winner for every position up to 100
nudges: What did the chocolate, the board of numbers and the heaps have in common?
steps.showed: Look for the counter: pieces, numbers, heaps, edges. If every move ticks it by one, the game is already decided.

steps.prompt: In such a game a problem says "both play optimally". What role does optimal play have?
options: None: every sequence of moves gives the same winner
It only matters for the second player
nudges: Could a bad move change the number of moves in the game?
steps.showed: The phrase is there for every game; in a fixed-length game it changes nothing.

steps.prompt: A game starts with one heap of $n \ge 1$ stones. A move splits one heap into two non-empty heaps; a player who cannot move loses. Prove that the game always lasts exactly $n - 1$ moves.
claims: Each move replaces one heap by two, so the number of heaps increases by exactly one per move.
A move is possible exactly when some heap has at least two stones, so the game ends precisely when every heap has one stone, that is, when there are n heaps.
The number of heaps goes from 1 to n in steps of one, so exactly n - 1 moves are made, whatever the players choose.
nudges: What changes by exactly one with every move?
What does the position look like when nobody can move?
steps.showed: Count heaps: one more each move, from 1 up to n.

reveal.name: Games of fixed length
reveal.statement: If some quantity changes by exactly one with every move and the game ends exactly when it reaches a fixed value, then every play has the same number of moves and the winner is decided by its parity alone.
reveal.remark: It is the game-theory face of an invariant. Many "who wins?" problems at the easy end of a contest are this in disguise: count moves, do not search for strategy.
